findings.title: Queries are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)
findings.body: `runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but each resulting sub-request is executed via `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)` → `super.query()` (`DataSourceWithBackend.query`), which already calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every target. So each split query is interpolated at least twice. Two concrete consequences: (1) ad hoc filters (`request.filters`) are applied by `addAdHocFilters()` a second time to an expression that already contains them, which can duplicate label matchers / pipeline stages (e.g. `| key="value" | key="value"`); (2) `templateSrv.replace()` runs again over values that were already substituted, so any variable whose value contains `$name`, `${name}` or `[[name]]` is expanded a second time and the final LogQL is wrong. If the interpolated query is only needed to make splitting decisions (step parsing, logs-vs-metric classification, `$__range` detection), keep it locally for those decisions and send the original targets downstream, or mark the request/targets as already interpolated so the backend data source layer skips the second pass.

findings.title: Shard splitting path now interpolates each query three times
findings.body: `runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here; `splitQueriesByStreamShard` then builds `subRequest` from those interpolated + shard-annotated targets and hands it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which after this PR interpolates again, and `runQuery`/`DataSourceWithBackend.query` interpolates a third time. Besides the correctness problems of repeated interpolation (ad hoc filters re-appended to an expression that already carries them, template values containing `$`/`${}`/`[[]]` re-expanded), the expression handed to the 2nd/3rd pass already contains the injected `__stream_shard__=~"..." | drop __stream_shard__`, so `addAdHocFilters()` re-parses and re-modifies a mutated query whose stage ordering is no longer the user's. There is also avoidable cost: `addAdHocFilters` parses the LogQL expression per target, now once per shard group in addition to the per-sub-request pass.

findings.title: Test asserts applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single target, locking in redundant interpolation
findings.body: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` is for a request with a single target. The 5 calls come from one interpolation in `runShardSplitQuery` plus one per sub-request created by `runSplitQuery`, i.e. the assertion codifies that the same query is interpolated repeatedly instead of exactly once. This makes the test both a brittle magic number (it changes whenever the shard grouping or the number of split requests changes) and a guard that prevents noticing the double/triple interpolation problem. The intent of the test ("Interpolates queries before running") would be better expressed by asserting interpolation happened once per user target.

findings.title: applyTemplateVariables mock mutates the query and is idempotent, masking repeated interpolation
findings.body: The new mock `datasource.applyTemplateVariables = jest.fn().mockImplementation((query) => { query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', '{a="b"}'); return query; })` mutates the target object in place and performs a replacement that is a no-op the second time it runs. The real implementation returns a new object and is *not* idempotent (it re-applies ad hoc filters and re-runs template replacement). Because of this mock, the tests cannot detect that the same target is now interpolated multiple times, and they also silently mutate the shared `request.targets` fixture used by subsequent assertions in the same test.

findings.title: New interpolation test is unrealistic and does not cover the risk introduced
findings.body: The stubbed `replace: (input = '') => input.replace('$__auto', '5m').replace('$step', '5m')` ignores `scopedVars`, whereas the real Loki `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__range` from the scoped vars so that these are interpolated by the backend; so in production `$__auto` is still present in the expression at this point and the assertion `expr === 'count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])'` does not reflect real behavior. More importantly, the actual risk of this change — the target being interpolated again by `DataSourceWithBackend.query` inside `runQuery`, duplicating ad hoc filters from `request.filters` and re-expanding variable values that contain `$` — is untested. Add a test with `request.filters` set asserting the ad hoc filter appears exactly once in the final expression sent to `runQuery`, and one with a variable value containing `$`/`${}` to assert it is not re-expanded.
